title: Append-only
text:
Many data structures and databases implement immutable objects, effectively making their data structures append-only. Implementing an append-only data structure has many benefits, such as ensuring data consistency, improving performance,[1] and permitting rollbacks.[2,3]

The prototypical append-only data structure is the log file. Log-structured data structures found in Log-structured file systems and databases work in a similar way: every change (transaction) that happens to the data is logged by the program, and on retrieval the program must combine the pieces of data found in this log file.[4] Blockchains add cryptography to the logs so that every transaction is verifiable.

Append-only data structures may also be mandated by the hardware or software environment:

All objects are immutable in purely functional programming languages, where every function is pure and global states do not exist.[5]

Flash storage pages can only be written to ("programmed") once before erasing. Erasing on a flash drive works on the level of "blocks", which cover hundreds to thousands of pages, so each block is treated as an append-only set of pages.[4,6]

Hard drives that use shingled magnetic recording cannot be written to randomly because writing on a track would clobber a neighboring, usually later, track. As a result, each "zone" on the drive is append-only.[7,1]

Append-only data structures grow over time, with more and more space dedicated to "stale" data found only in the history and more time wasted on parsing these data. A number of append-only systems implement rewriting (copying garbage collection), so that a new structure is created only containing the current version and optionally a few older ones.[2,8]
